title: Elastic concurrency & queue-pressure cheatsheet for batching
content:
Purpose:
Short, pragmatic reference for sizing concurrency and batch targets when using continuous/elastic batching. Focus is on how queue pressure affects p95 latency and unit token cost, plus a set of quick knobs and spreadsheet columns to capture sensitivity tests.

Context / motivation:
- Ops teams want a repeatable mapping: observed qps (or token-qps) -> recommended node concurrency + batch_target.
- We trade off: lower token cost (bigger batches) vs higher p95 (wait-for-batch). Under bursty traffic the queue can blow up and p95 spikes.
- This doc is intentionally rough: contains quick heuristics and example scenarios we can paste into the cost spreadsheet.

Quick recommendations (opinionated):
- Target steady-state: configure batch_target to capture 60–80% of peak instantaneous request arrival bursts. This usually maps to median batch utilization ~0.6.
- Concurrency as a safety multiplier: set concurrency = ceil( (expected_qps * avg_tokens_per_request * token_service_ms) / (gpu_tokens_per_ms) * 1.25 ). Use 1.25–1.5 multiplier if latency SLO is strict.
- Max queue threshold: trigger autoscale/fallback when queue length > 2 * batch_target for >30s.
- P95 SLO buffer: aim for queue-wait contribution <= 40% of p95 budget. If p95 budget is 500ms, target queue wait <=200ms.

Heuristic formulas (put these in spreadsheet cells):
- avg_batch_wait_ms ≈ 0.5 * batch_target / arrival_rate_rps * avg_request_tokens_factor
  - Rationale: continuous batching waits for enough arrivals to fill batch; expected wait ~ half the time to fill the target.
- effective_service_ms_per_request ≈ model_service_ms_per_token * avg_tokens + batch_overhead_ms / batch_fill_size
- p95_estimate_ms ≈ queue_wait_ms_95 + effective_service_ms * safety_factor(1.1–1.5) + network_ms_estimate

Simple queueing intuition (for spreadsheet):
- arrival_rate = requests_per_sec (rps)
- service_rate_per_worker = 1 / (effective_service_per_request_in_sec)
- offered_load = arrival_rate / (concurrency * service_rate_per_worker)
  - If offered_load >= 1 -> queue unstable (unbounded). Flag immediately.

Example scenarios (copy into sensitivity sheet):
Scenario A — low-latency chat (p95 target 250ms):
- avg_tokens = 30, model_service_ms_per_token = 1.2 ms, batch_overhead_ms = 6 ms
- arrival_rate = 35 rps
- Try batch_target=8 -> avg_batch_wait ≈ 0.5 * 8 / 35 ≈ 114 ms
  - effective_service ≈ 1.2*30 + 6/8 ≈ 36 + 0.75 ≈ 36.75 ms
  - p95 ≈ 114 + 36.75*1.25 ≈ 184 ms -> within budget (good)
- If batch_target=32 -> avg_batch_wait ≈ 0.5 * 32 / 35 ≈ 457 ms -> p95 ≈ 457 + 36.75*1.25 ≈ 527 ms -> misses SLO
- Recommendation: batch_target=8, concurrency minimal + 20% headroom

Scenario B — throughput-first embeddings (p95 target 1s but cost sensitive):
- avg_tokens = 1024, model_service_ms_per_token = 0.09 ms (vector model fast per token), batch_overhead_ms = 10 ms, arrival_rate = 10 rps
- batch_target=64 -> avg_batch_wait ≈ 0.5 * 64 / 10 ≈ 3.2 s (bad)
- batch_target=8 -> avg_batch_wait ≈ 0.5 * 8 / 10 ≈ 400 ms
- effective_service per request dominates at larger tokens; prefer smaller batch_target and scale concurrency to keep unit cost reasonable.

Cheat table: (paste into sheet for quick mapping)
- <10 rps: batch_target = max(8, ceil(0.8 * expected_rps_to_fill_batch)), concurrency = baseline_nodes(1)
- 10–50 rps: batch_target = 8–12 for chat-like tokens (<=100 tokens); concurrency = ceil( (rps * avg_tokens * token_ms) / gpu_token_capacity_ms ) * 1.25
- 50–200 rps: favor smaller batch_target (6–10) and more concurrency to avoid long waits; consider KV prefix caching for repeated starting tokens
- >200 rps: continuous batching pays off; tune scheduling to form multi-batch kernels and increase concurrency aggressively

Spreadsheet column suggestions (single-row per scenario):
- scenario_name, arrival_rps, avg_tokens, tokens_per_sec, token_ms, batch_target, avg_batch_wait_ms, batch_fill_size_estimate, effective_service_ms, concurrency_recommended, offered_load, p95_estimate_ms, unit_cost_per_1k_tokens, notes

Sensitivity tests to run (add to cost spreadsheet):
- Vary CV (coefficient of variation) of inter-arrival from 0.2 -> 2.0; record p95 and 99.
- Simulate burst: baseline rps * 5 for 60s every 15m; see queue build-up and tail latency.
- Vary model_service_ms_per_token +/- 25% (quantization or kernel differences).
- Test effect of batch_target doubling and halving on token cost (measure CPU/GPU utilization and throughput).

Operational knobs and fallback policies:
- Emergency fallback chain: (1) temporary lower-precision model variant (faster tokens), (2) reduce batch_target to prioritise latency, (3) route to lower-cost region with spare capacity.
- Autoscale triggers: queue_length > 2*batch_target for 30s OR offered_load >= 0.9 for 60s -> add concurrency +1 node.
- Backpressure: if queue_length > 10*batch_target, return 429 or degrade non-essential requests (e.g., telemetry).

Open questions / TODOs (working):
- Validate avg_batch_wait formula against trace-based simulator for heavy-tailed inter-arrival distributions. (Ling to run sim)
- Add per-model kernel-level batch merge efficiency to spreadsheet (some models get >1.6x throughput when kernel-merging).
- Compute exact cost delta when reducing batch_target by 2x for common customer workloads (Ravi owns).

Notes to self / shortcuts used in spreadsheet cells:
- Use a 95th-percentile arrival-based wait estimate: queue_wait_95 ≈ 2x median wait for moderate CV, 4x for heavy tail.
- When in doubt, prefer concurrency over huge batch_target; users notice latency spikes more than token-cost micro-savings.

References / quick links:
- Elastic batching cost sheet: https://docs.google.com/spreadsheets/d/elastic-batching-costs-v2
- Jira: JIRA-OPS-1245 (autoscale + queue policy)

Bottom line / one-liner for on-call: "If p95 climbs and offered_load < 0.9 then lower batch_target; if offered_load >= 0.9 scale up. Prefer smaller batches under bursty traffic. Track queue_length relative to batch_target as primary alarm."
